entry: Natural light display in Earth's upper atmosphere, caused by charged particles from the [[Sun]] colliding with atoms in the atmosphere. The collisions excite [[Oxygen|oxygen]] and [[Nitrogen|nitrogen]], which emit light of different colors such as green, red and purple. Auroras appear as curtains, rays, spirals or dynamic flickers and are most commonly observed in a band approximately 6° (~660 km) wide in latitude, centered on 67° north and south. They are called the northern lights (aurora borealis) in the [[Arctic]] and the southern lights (aurora australis) in the Antarctic. Auroras result from disturbances in Earth's magnetosphere caused by enhanced speeds of [[Solar wind|solar wind]] from coronal holes and coronal mass ejections. The name derives from Aurora, the Roman goddess of the dawn. Other planets, [[Brown dwarf|brown dwarfs]], [[Comet|comets]] and some natural satellites also host auroras.

Complex of over 40 concentration and extermination camps in occupied Poland, operated by [[Nazi Germany]] during [[World War II]] and the Holocaust. Of the 1.3 million people sent to Auschwitz, 1.1 million were murdered, including 960,000 [[Jews]]. From 1942 until late 1944, freight trains delivered Jews from across German-occupied Europe to its gas chambers. Soviet troops liberated the camp on 27 January 1945. The Allies' failure to bomb the camp or its railways remains controversial. Auschwitz is the site of the largest mass murder in a single location in history.

City (pop., 2020: 961,855), capital of [[Texas]], United States. Austin is the county seat of Travis County and has been one of the fastest-growing large cities in the United States since 2010. Since the 1990s it has been a center for technology and business, and Fortune 500 companies with headquarters or regional offices there include [[Dell]], [[IBM]] and [[Intel]]. Home to the University of Texas at Austin, the city hosts South by Southwest (SXSW), an annual festival of film, interactive media and music. Its slogan is "The Live Music Capital of the World."

Geographical subregion of [[Oceania]] with ambiguous extents. Australasia always includes [[Australia]] and [[New Zealand]], and often also includes [[New Guinea]]. In its broadest sense it may include the entire [[Malay Archipelago]]. Usage varies; in New Zealand it often denotes only Australia and New Zealand. Charles de Brosses coined the term in French as *Australasie* in *Histoire des navigations aux terres australes* (1756).

Smallest of the seven traditional continents, comprising the Australian mainland, [[Tasmania]] and the island of [[New Guinea]]. It is also known in technical contexts as Sahul, Australia-New Guinea, Australinea or Meganesia, to distinguish it from the country. When sea levels were lower, including during the [[Last Glacial Maximum]] about 18,000 BC, the landmasses were joined by dry land as Sahul. Rising [[Sea level|sea levels]] over the past 18,000 to 10,000 years separated them into today's continent. With a total land area of 8.56 million square kilometers (3,310,000 sq mi), it is the smallest, lowest, flattest and second-driest continent, after [[Antarctica]]. The continental shelf is overlain by shallow seas, including the Arafura Sea and Torres Strait between mainland Australia and New Guinea, and Bass Strait between mainland Australia and Tasmania. Its mainland is low-lying and arid to semi-arid.

Sacred spirituality expressed in the stories that [[Aboriginal Australians]] perform in ceremonies within each language group across Australia. It includes the Dreaming, songlines and [[Oral tradition|oral literature]]. Most spiritualities belong to specific groups, though some span the whole continent. Aboriginal stories often describe each group's local landscape, giving cultural meaning to its topography. Some myths preserve memories of geological events. Myths about the Crater Lakes of the Atherton Tableland describe their volcanic origin, which geological research dated to more than 10,000 years ago; pollen in the crater silt showed that eucalyptus forests dominated when the craters formed. Myths about the deserts around Lake Eyre describe them as once well-watered, matching geologists' understanding of a wet phase in the early [[Holocene]].

Australian public broadcaster providing news, current affairs, factual and entertainment programming across television, radio and the web. Founded in 1932, it has been taxpayer-funded since 1949. Its remit requires political independence, but critics have alleged left-leaning bias in its news and current affairs. Its postal address in every Australian capital city is PO Box 9994, a tribute to the record-breaking Test batting average of cricketer [[Don Bradman]].

Family of mygalomorph [[Spider|spiders]] native to [[Australia]], comprising three genera (*Atrax*, *Hadronyche* and *Illawarra*) and 35 species. Spiders in the family have body lengths of 1 to 5 cm and build burrows in moist, sheltered habitats. Their primary range is the eastern coast, in [[New South Wales]], [[Queensland]], [[South Australia]], [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]] and [[Tasmania]]. Some species have venom dangerous to humans. The bites of the Sydney funnel-web spider (*Atrax robustus*) and northern tree-dwelling funnel-web spider (*Hadronyche formidabilis*) are potentially deadly, but no fatalities have occurred since the introduction of modern first-aid techniques and antivenom.

Contact sport played between two teams of 18 players on an oval field, often a modified [[Cricket|cricket]] ground. Points are scored by kicking the oval ball between the central goal posts (worth six points) or between a central and outer post (worth one point, known as a behind). A distinctive feature is the mark, in which a player who catches a kick under specific conditions is awarded unimpeded possession. The sport originated in [[Melbourne]], Victoria, in 1858, when football games inspired by English public school games were organized. The Melbourne Football Club published the first laws in May 1859. The sport has the highest spectator attendance of all sports in Australia. The Australian Football League (AFL) is its only fully professional competition, and its Grand Final is held annually at the 100,024-capacity Melbourne Cricket Ground.

Extinct genus of early hominins that lived in Africa during the [[Pliocene]] and Early Pleistocene. Species include *A. anamensis*, *A. afarensis* and *A. africanus*. The earliest known member, *A. anamensis*, existed in eastern Africa around 4.2 million years ago. The genus became extinct 1.9 million years ago, or 1.2 to 0.6 million years ago if [[Paranthropus]] is included. The genus [[Homo]], which includes modern [[Human|humans]], evolved from some Australopithecus species between 3 and 2 million years ago. The type specimen, the skull of a three-year-old nicknamed the Taung Child, was found in 1924 in a lime quarry in South Africa and first reported in [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] in February 1925. The partial skeleton [[Lucy (hominid)|Lucy]] of *A. afarensis*, found in 1974 in Ethiopia, is the best-known specimen.

Landlocked country in Central Europe, lying in the Eastern Alps and organized as a federation of nine states. Its capital, [[Vienna]], is the most populous city. Austria covers 83,879 sq km (32,386 sq mi) and has a population of about 9.2 million. The area was inhabited from the Paleolithic period and annexed by the [[Roman Empire]] in the late 1st century BC. It became a duchy in 1156 and was the heartland of the [[Habsburg monarchy]] from the late 13th century. Austria was part of [[Austria-Hungary]] from 1867 until 1918 and was annexed into [[Nazi Germany]] in 1938. After liberation in 1945 and a decade of Allied occupation, it declared perpetual neutrality in 1955. It joined the [[United Nations]] in 1955 and the [[European Union]] in 1995, and adopted the [[Euro|euro]] in 1999.

Multinational dual monarchy in [[Central Europe]], 1867–1918. Formed by the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867 after the [[Austro-Prussian War]], it joined the [[Austrian Empire]] and the [[Kingdom of Hungary]] under one monarch, titled both Emperor of Austria and Apostolic King of Hungary. The two states were largely self-governing but shared diplomatic, defense and monetary policies. Austria-Hungary was the second-largest country in Europe by area, after [[Russia]]. It was one of the [[Central Powers]] in [[World War I]], which began with its declaration of war on the Kingdom of Serbia on 28 July 1914. The union was dissolved in 1918 after Hungary terminated it.

Multinational European great power, 1804–1867, created by proclamation out of the realms of the [[Habsburg monarchy|Habsburgs]]. Francis II proclaimed it in 1804 in response to [[Napoleon]]'s declaration of the [[First French Empire]], uniting all Habsburg possessions under one central government. It remained part of the [[Holy Roman Empire]] until that empire's dissolution in 1806. Austria fought Napoleon in the Napoleonic Wars except between 1809 and 1813, and emerged victorious; the [[Congress of Vienna]] reaffirmed it as one of the great powers of the 19th century. After defeat in the [[Austro-Prussian War]] of 1866, the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867 joined it with the Kingdom of Hungary to form [[Austria-Hungary]].

Brief war of 1866 between the [[Austrian Empire]] and the [[Kingdom of Prussia]], also known as the Seven Weeks' War. Prussia's victory shifted power among the German states from Austria to Prussia. The war abolished the [[German Confederation]], partly replacing it with the North German Confederation, which excluded Austria. The [[Kingdom of Italy]], allied with Prussia, gained the Austrian realm of Venetia. The decisive battle was at Königgrätz (Sadowa) on 3 July 1866.

Large [[Language family|language family]] spoken throughout [[Mainland Southeast Asia]], [[South Asia]] and [[East Asia]]. About 117 million people speak an Austroasiatic language, more than two-thirds of them Vietnamese speakers. Only Vietnamese, [[Khmer language|Khmer]] and Mon have lengthy written records. Vietnamese and Khmer are the national languages of [[Vietnam]] and [[Cambodia]]. Ethnologue identifies 168 languages, traditionally grouped into two branches, Mon–Khmer and Munda. Scholars generally date the ancestral language to c. 3000 BC–c. 2000 BC, with a homeland in Mainland Southeast Asia or southern China.

Large [[Language family|language family]] widely spoken across Maritime Southeast Asia, [[Madagascar]], the islands of the [[Pacific Ocean]] and [[Taiwan]]. Its speakers number approximately 386 million, or 4.4% of the [[World population|world population]], making it the fifth-largest family by number of speakers. According to some estimates it contains 1,257 languages, the second most of any family. Major languages include Malay (standardized as Indonesian), Javanese, Tagalog (standardized as Filipino), Malagasy and Cebuano. Indonesian, the most widely spoken, has around 252 million speakers. The family ranges from Madagascar to [[Easter Island]]. All Austronesian languages spoken outside Taiwan belong to the Malayo-Polynesian branch. The oldest inscription in the Cham language dates to c. 350 AD.

Peoples who speak [[Austronesian languages]], settled across Taiwan, maritime Southeast Asia, Micronesia, Melanesia, Polynesia and Madagascar. They trace their origin to a prehistoric seaborne expansion from Taiwan, c. 3000 to 1500 BC. Austronesians reached the Batanes Islands in the northernmost [[Philippines]] by around 2200 BC and used sails before 2000 BC. Using catamarans, outrigger boats and lashed-lug boats, they dispersed to Easter Island, Madagascar, New Zealand and Hawaii, and settled New Zealand c. 1250. Shared traditions include lashed-lug shipbuilding, tattooing, stilt houses, jade carving, wetland agriculture and rock art. Domesticated plants carried along the migrations include [[Rice]], bananas, coconuts, breadfruit, Dioscorea yams and [[Taro]].

Act of proving that something, such as an identity, document, work of art or financial transaction, is genuine, valid or true. In contrast with identification, which indicates a person's or thing's identity, authentication verifies that identity. In art, antiques and anthropology it establishes whether an artifact is counterfeit or from a given period, as by carbon dating. In [[Computer science|computing]], it verifies the identity of a user, process or device, often as a prerequisite to access to confidential data or systems. Methods fall into three factors: something known (such as [[Password|passwords]] or PINs), something possessed (such as smart cards or tokens), and something inherent (such as fingerprints or facial recognition). Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires at least two distinct factors.

Neurodevelopmental condition, also called autism spectrum disorder (ASD), characterized by impaired social communication and interaction and by a need for predictability, sensory processing differences, focused interests or repetitive behaviors. Features are present from early childhood and typically persist throughout life; support needs range from minimal assistance to full-time, 24-hour care. The [[World Health Organization]] estimates that about 1 in 100 children were diagnosed between 2012 and 2021, an increasing trend. Autism is highly heritable and involves many genes, while environmental factors appear to play a smaller, mainly prenatal role. Boys are diagnosed several times more often than girls. There is no cure. Therapies aim to improve self-care, social and language skills, and medication can help manage co-occurring conditions such as [[Anxiety|anxiety]], [[Depression (mood)|depression]] and [[Epilepsy|epilepsy]]. The neurodiversity framework views autistic traits as a healthy variation of the human condition; this view is debated and remains controversial.

Motorsport involving the racing of automobiles for competition. Races were organized from the invention of the automobile, the first recorded in 1867, and many early events were reliability trials. Specialist racing cars had developed by the 1930s. The first formal Grand Prix was held in 1906 at Le Mans, France, over a 105 km circuit, and was won by Ferenc Szisz in a Renault. The sport is regulated internationally by the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), founded in 1904. Disciplines include open-wheel racing, stock car racing as in [[NASCAR]], sports car endurance events, rallying and drag racing. [[Formula One]] is the pinnacle of open-wheel racing; its inaugural World Championship was held in 1950.

Federal controlled-access [[Controlled-access highway|highway]] system in [[Germany]]. Officially called Bundesautobahn (BAB, 'federal motorway'), it spans approximately 13,192 km and connects major cities across all 16 federal states. Much of it has no speed limit for some vehicle classes, although an advisory speed of 130 km/h applies on unrestricted stretches. The AVUS racetrack-cum-motorway near [[Berlin]], built between 1913 and 1921, was the world's first such facility. Environmental impacts and accident risks remain subjects of controversy.

Self-written account of one's own life, narrated from the author's perspective. The term was first used in 1797, but the practice dates to antiquity. Unlike [[Biography|biographies]], which are written by someone else, autobiographies rest on the author's memory and interpretation of events, so they may contain inaccuracies or embellishments. Early examples include Saint Augustine's *Confessions* (c. 400), often considered one of the first Western autobiographies. *The Book of Margery Kempe* (c. 1430s) is considered the first autobiography in English. [[Benjamin Franklin]]'s *The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin* (written 1771–1790, published 1791) exemplifies Enlightenment self-improvement narratives. Forms include memoirs, which focus on specific periods or themes, spiritual autobiographies and fictional first-person autobiographies.

Form of government in which absolute power is held by one person, known as an autocrat. It includes absolute monarchies and dictatorships and is contrasted with [[Democracy|democracy]]. Autocrats maintain power through political repression and co-optation of influential figures, while the public is controlled through indoctrination and [[Propaganda|propaganda]]. Mixed regimes that blend autocracy and democracy are sometimes called anocracy, hybrid regime or electoral autocracy. Autocracy was among the earliest forms of government. [[Monarchy]] was the predominant form for most of history, and [[Dictatorship|dictatorship]] became more common in the 19th century, beginning with the caudillos in Latin America and the empires of [[Napoleon|Napoleon I]] and [[Napoleon III]]. Totalitarian dictatorships developed in the 20th century with fascist and communist states.

Disease resulting from an anomalous response of the adaptive [[Immune system|immune system]], which mistakenly attacks healthy, functioning parts of the body. More than 80 autoimmune diseases are recognized, and nearly any body part can be involved. Unlike autoinflammatory diseases, which involve the innate immune system, they stem from a malfunction of the adaptive system. Symptoms vary but typically include low-grade fever, fatigue and general malaise. Common examples include [[Rheumatoid arthritis]], [[Lupus|systemic lupus erythematosus]], [[Multiple sclerosis]] and [[Psoriasis]], as well as type 1 diabetes, in which the immune system destroys insulin-producing cells in the [[Pancreas|pancreas]]. Causes are unclear and likely involve both genetic and environmental influences. Treatments use nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and immunosuppressants to reduce immune activity, but they usually do not offer a cure. Women are more commonly affected than men.

Range of technologies that reduce human intervention in processes by predetermining decision criteria and actions and embodying them in [[Machine|machines]]. Automation has been achieved through mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, electrical and electronic devices, and [[Computer|computers]], usually in combination. Its benefits include labor savings, reduced waste, and improvements in quality, accuracy and precision. The simplest automatic control loop compares a measured value of a process with a desired set value and adjusts the process to hold its set point despite disturbances. The term was not widely used before 1947, when Ford established an automation department. Industrial [[Industrial robot|robots]] were introduced in the 1960s. A 2019 World Bank report found that technology-sector jobs outweigh the economic effects of workers displaced by automation.
